Timorous

TIM-er-us · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Timorous is fearful, easily frightened, or nervous.

The timorous kitten spent its first week in the new house hiding under the couch, flinching at every footstep.

Worked Example

Timorous by nature, the new hire double-checked every email three times before sending it, terrified of making a visible mistake.

Being generally nervous and easily frightened, even by small everyday risks, is exactly what timorous describes.

How Strong Is It? — fainthearted → timorous → skittish

fainthearted vs. timorous

fainthearted vs. timorous: Fainthearted is milder than timorous: a fainthearted climber backs out of one risky climb, while a timorous person is more deeply fearful, frightened by almost everything almost all the time.

skittish vs. timorous

skittish vs. timorous: The skittish colt bolted at the sound of the gate creaking, nearly throwing its rider.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — tim-

root — tim-: fear (Latin)

suffix — -orous

suffix — -orous: full of, characterized by (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Timorous comes from Latin timor, 'fear,' plus the adjective-forming suffix -orous, 'full of.' Someone timorous is, quite literally, full of fear.

Where it comes from

Where it comes from: Latin packed a whole description into this word: timor ('fear') plus -orous ('full of') spells out 'full of fear.' When you meet timorous in a sentence, you can unpack it on the spot -- the parts still mean exactly what they say.

Root Check

Word Choice

Timorous describes a general, everyday nervousness or easily-startled temperament -- it doesn't carry the moral judgment of pusillanimous (which implies a shameful failure of courage) or the social self-doubt of diffident (which is about hesitating to speak up, not fear of danger at all).
